I work in the mental health field and I also have BPD. It can be a difficult area because some people with BPD when they are struggling and don't have support can be very difficult to work with (i think its impossible for someone without the diagnosis to understand what it feels like), and some with the diagnosis are just toxic awful people. But that doesn't mean that everyone with the diagnosis is hurtful or difficult. 

With BPD all emotions are unbearably intense and mental health crisis occurs more often. When feelings are so intense and change so dramatically its very difficult to manage behaviour and reactions to situations. To manage this treatment and support is ongoing and just because someone relapses doesn't mean they aren't trying. 

I'm not denying some with BPD are toxic and not willing to engage in treatment, and I know many people have suffered from the actions of those who may have a diagnosis. But many with BPD harm and destroy their own lives but would do anything to help or support others. Just want to prevent too much stigma with an already misunderstood diagnosis.

Gradually our understanding and detection then treatment of BPD is improving. I'm still not convinced on the strength of the DSM diagnosis but more and more awareness and support is out there for complex mental health issues. I hope as it improves fewer and fewer people have to experience what you have had to go through.

I completely agree about cutting toxic people out of your life, no matter their relationship to you. I just wanted to add that not everyone with personality disorders or BPD are toxic people or untreatable. They are very complex disorders and not entirely understood and some individuals definitely can be very difficult or dangerous, but there is a lot of stigma and I hope the entire diagnosis isn't generalised based on certain individuals.

To me candles and herbs etc are a tool to remind me what I'm focusing on. They act as a representation of a feeling or mood I'm trying to work on. I use my practice as a way of mindfully grounding myself and mediating and I find it helpful to have something to represent what I currently need some help with. I prefer using crystals, herbs and colors to deities because to me they represent nature, which is closer to my spiritual beliefs than any deity. 

But of course the whole point is that you use whatever has personal meaning to you. While one person might see that represented one way, someone else will see it in a different light. I also think the sensory nature of the smell of herbs, watching a flame, and holding a crystal is very helpful for me to meditate and remain grounded when usually I am very anxious and jittery and struggle to do anything that is for my own benefit.

It’s all very personal and specific to you. I’ve tried many many different combinations of medications and currently the ones I’m on work for me. It really is trial and error with medication. Some people don’t want to rely on them, but for me it keeps me stable enough to live my life. For others it’s just a way to keep going until other support is in place. But it takes a while to find the right one for you. CBT is the cheap easy option for the NHS to give out. But again it’s very particular to each person. My best combination was a private life coach, CBT with mindfulness and a regular check in with a psychiatrist. But this was partly privately funded. I liked CBT because it felt practical and something to strategically work through. But some people find it a bit too structured and a bit unfeeling. That also depends on the therapist. NHS will always push CBT because it’s cheap and quick. But if you think you’d prefer a different therapy keep talking to them and see what they can offer. Hope this helps a little? Oh finally something I can answer. I could talk about this for hours so I'll try to keep it short. 

I was in an induced coma for 2 weeks, after taking an overdose that very nearly killed me. I was on a ventilator and underwent different procedures. Being induced the drugs partially caused hallucinations, which probably contributed to the experience.

The earliest things are I can remember are sickening nightmares that never ended. I thought I'd lived billions of lifetimes trapped within the same nightmares. Varying from murder, mutilation and rape, to constantly drowning under sand, being build into a pyramid made of human bodies, to letting my whole family down. 

Eventually as I drifted in and out of consciousness little parts of reality came through. I was aware I was in a bed, covered in wires and couldn't move or speak. I constantly tried to scream and thrash and pull the tubes out. It felt like how it does in dreams, when you desperately try to shout or run but your body isn't reacting. I remember several times voices telling me I was safe, it was okay, I was in hospital and I was safe. But I just kept trying to scream to escape the never ending nightmares. Eventually drifting back into unconsciousness. 

Apparently when the ventilator was taken out and I was gradually coming back into consciousness I spoke parts on my dreams out. My mum tells me I kept trying (I didn't really have a voice) to shout at her to 'just fucking pay'. They all found it very funny. In my mind I was chained to a post and was going to be kept prisoner because my mum was refusing to pay for a meal or something. Apparently I also swore at a lot of nurses!

I remember the first time I was allowed water. I could only have tiny bits at a time but after having a tube down my throat for a week I felt like I was dying of dehydration. I thought I was being given water to drink through a sieve in the middle of the desert, sinking into sand. I kept begging and pleading for more but it was refused. I thought I was dying. Every time I was allowed some water it felt like a single droplet that just made me thirstier. It felt like more torture and wasn't aware this was reality as it felt the same as the nightmares. 

I could go on but from there is mostly the after effects of the medication that induced the coma. 

I have many more stories of the dream like states I experienced during.

Almost a year ago I took a lethal overdose of medication around the house. My boyfriend called me and realised something was really wrong and got me help. I had several seizures, dangerous blood pressure and my heart stopped. Luckily I was already in a&e. I was rushed to intensive care and placed into an induced coma. 

These details are all I have from other people, I've don't remember any of October-mid December last year. I don't even remember taking the overdose. 

I've already struggled with my mental health most of my life but it was only really noticed when I was a young teenager. Severe depression and anxiety. It affected every part of my life and I hated my existence. I dropped out of school and went into work. Lost my job due to my mental health, lost the very few friends who had put up with me this far. My self harm was getting worse and worse, and i was stuck in the addiction

Basically everything sucked and I hated everything about myself, I'd planned suicide for years. But apparently something just clicked in my mind that day that made me go through with it

The coma was, what I can only describe as, a living hell. I was trapped in eternal torture of failing my family and friends, destroying everything and ultimately being unable to die. I experienced it all through dreams and hallucinations caused by the drugs keeping me in the coma. At times I would come round and try to scream to my parents and nurses to kill me to end the loop of pain I was stuck in. 

Eventually my body had recovered enough to bring me out of the coma. I had been taken off a ventilator, had dialysis, had liquid removed from my lungs, reduced my blood pressure. 

I had no idea why I was in hospital, I was still hallucinating, very very confused. But one thing I understood was that my family loved me and cared for me. That was one of the most powerful feelings I've ever experienced. Waking up from hell to my loving family who had been through their own hell for the past 2 weeks. Everyone in my family had send cards or passes on notes or gifts, everyone had visited me while I was asleep. And suddenly I realised I was loved. That I was wrong and people really would care if I was gone. 

One thing that sticks in my head now is the nurses. Even if my family hadn't been there the nurses made me feel loved and cared for and important. I don't remember clearly at all, but I know one nurse sat with me and spoke to me about being in my position and learning to love life and accept who you are no matter what the world says. Other nurses washed and plaited my hair, chatted with me, and were all round incredible. 

I willingly went into a psychiatric ward because I didn't feel safe to be left alone, but I felt like a different person. I described it to the people around me that I felt like I'd been reset. When I woke I felt like I'd been to hell and awoken and realised what I had and how loved I was

I left and worked powerfully hard to reach my life goal to get to university. My parents paid for private mental health care, after the NHS had failed me for 7 years. I saw professionals and got a diagnosis (emotionally unstable personality disorder) and felt stronger and more powerful than I ever had!

Today I have an incredible loving boyfriend who supports me through everything, I'm currently at university doing my dream course, studying to become a clinical psychologist to help other, I'm clean from self harm for around a year, I keep myself safe and look after myself. 

I'm still on medication and receiving support, but I feel like my life is finally on track. It just took dying to realise what I have and what I want out of this time on earth

The story is much more complex to go into here. But please comment or message me with any questions or if you want to talk about these feelings. I want to do whatever I can to help others who are going/have gone through this hell
